recruitment.note: Every dynamic credential comes out with a lease on it, and when the lease expires Vault revokes it whether or not anybody remembered to.
You write the end state. The plan is the difference between what you wrote and what is really out there.
A catalog of services with a health check beside every entry, and a DNS name in front of the pair.
A Vagrantfile, one vagrant up, and the same development machine on everybody's laptop. Older than the company that makes it.
Policy as code, with the verdict kept out of the policy: advisory warns, soft mandatory can be overridden, hard mandatory cannot.
You ask for a target and get a session. The hosts behind the target come out of a catalog you never have to read.
A job file says what to run and how much of it. Which client it lands on is the scheduler's problem, not yours.

unseal.note: The half of the run that changes nothing. Game 1 is named after both halves, and only one of them is safe.
What Vault keeps beside a dynamic secret: how long it is good for, and whether you may ask for longer.
The process on every member of a Consul or Nomad cluster. A server runs one too; a flag is all that makes it a server.
What Nomad calls a client when the scheduler is the one talking. nomad node status is how you find out one stopped answering.

unseal.cue: R U Q M O U
unseal.note: Half the servers plus one. Lose it and Raft commits nothing, which is a cluster that is up and can no longer be written to.

unseal.cue: C Y L O P I
unseal.note: Vault denies by default, so this is the list of paths you are allowed and what you may do at each one. An empty one grants nothing.

unseal.cue: T E R C E S
unseal.note: A KV entry, a database credential, a certificate. Vault keeps all three behind paths, and generates most of them on the way out.

unseal.cue: G R Y T S I R E
unseal.note: Where a provider or a module is published so that a configuration can name it instead of keeping a copy.

unseal.cue: C U O R E S R E
unseal.note: Terraform's unit of work: one block, one object, one entry in state.

unseal.cue: A L P M E T E T
unseal.note: What Packer builds from. The provisioners in it run inside the running machine, before it is turned into an image.

unseal.cue: G N I S I V O R P I N O
unseal.note: Turning an empty account into a running one. Packer's provisioners do the same job one layer in, before the image is sealed.

unseal.cue: C A I T U N E H T A N O T I
unseal.note: Vault checks you against something it does not own — GitHub, LDAP, AppRole — and hands back a token.

unseal.cue: R U T C A R F S I N T U R E
unseal.note: The word in front of as code. Every product on this board is a way of managing some of it.

panes.label: Packer Pre-Processors
panes.note: There are builders, provisioners and post-processors. Nothing is called a pre-processor.

panes.label: Packer Post-Processors
panes.note: It takes the artifact a builder produced and makes another one out of it: compress it, upload it, re-package it.

panes.label: Terraform Moved Blocks
panes.note: A moved block tells the plan that a resource has a new address, so a refactor is a rename in state and not a destroy and create.

panes.label: Terraform Renamed Blocks
panes.note: There is a moved block, and renaming is what it is for. There is nothing called a renamed block.

panes.label: Vault Response Wrapping
panes.note: The response goes into the cubbyhole of a single-use token, and the token is what travels. If it will not unwrap, somebody else already did.

panes.label: Vault Courier Tokens
panes.note: Vault has service tokens and batch tokens, and a wrapping token that carries one response. It has never had a courier.

panes.label: Consul Standing Queries
panes.note: The stored kind is real and this is very nearly its name. Consul calls them prepared.

panes.label: Consul Prepared Queries
panes.note: A query kept on the servers rather than in the caller, which can fail over to another datacenter when nothing healthy answers at home.

panes.label: Nomad Spread Blocks
panes.note: A spread block asks the scheduler to distribute allocations evenly over a node attribute instead of packing them in.

panes.label: Nomad Scatter Blocks
panes.note: Nomad has a spread block and it has an affinity block. It has never had a scatter.

panes.label: Boundary Session Brokers
panes.note: Boundary brokers credentials, and a worker proxies the session. Neither of those is called a session broker.

panes.label: Boundary Dynamic Host Catalogs
panes.note: A host catalog that asks the cloud what is behind a target instead of being told: a plugin per provider, and tags for the rules.

gganbu.cue: Versions Vault's KV v2 keeps per key by default
gganbu.note: 10 — and the write past the tenth permanently deletes the oldest. The mount sets it, and a key's own metadata can overrule the mount.
5 — a slack default that suits a small server, and the production guidance is to set it to 1. It scales every Raft timer, so it is also how long a lost leader goes unnoticed.

gganbu.cue: Unseal key shares Vault asks for by default
gganbu.note: 3 — of the five shares vault operator init prints, any three reconstruct the root key. Five is the number everyone remembers, and it is the other one.

gganbu.cue: The year IBM's acquisition of HashiCorp closed
gganbu.note: 2025 — February, ten months after it was announced. Half a room files this under the year of the announcement, which is what makes it a wager.
2021 — June, at HashiConf Europe. What 1.0 shipped was not a feature but a promise: upgrade anywhere inside 1.x and the workflow keeps working.

gganbu.cue: The year Packer was first released
gganbu.note: 2013 — the first project started at HashiCorp. Vagrant is older still, and older than the company.
